title: WHO Says 45% of Dementia Cases Are Preventable, Adds Air Pollution and Hearing Aids to Guidelines
excerpt: The World Health Organization's first major dementia prevention update since 2019 introduces air pollution as a new risk factor and recommends hearing aids to reduce cognitive decline, while warning against certain popular supplements.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • WHO estimates up to 45% of dementia cases are preventable through lifestyle changes.
  • Hearing aids are now recommended to reduce dementia risk, potentially preventing 7% of cases.
  • Air pollution is a new risk factor, linked to approximately 3% of global dementia cases.
  • WHO warns against using certain supplements for brain health unless deficiencies are diagnosed.

WHO guidelines update
  • Up to 45% of dementia risk is linked to modifiable factors including air pollution, hearing loss, physical inactivity and chronic disease, according to updated WHO guidelines released July 15.
  • The WHO now recommends hearing aids — not just hearing screening — as a strategy to reduce dementia risk, estimating that eliminating hearing loss could prevent 7% of cases worldwide.
  • Air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter (PM2.5), has been added as a new risk factor, with the WHO estimating it accounts for roughly 3% of global dementia cases.
  • The agency warns against taking vitamins B, E, omega-3 fatty acids and multivitamins for brain health unless a diagnosed deficiency exists, citing potential harm.

First Major Update in Seven Years

The World Health Organization released updated guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia on July 15, marking the first significant revision since 2019. The new guidance draws on seven years of accumulated evidence covering lifestyle changes, medical interventions and environmental factors that can delay or prevent the disease.

More than 57 million people worldwide live with dementia, and nearly 10 million new cases are diagnosed each year, according to the WHO. Alzheimer's disease accounts for 60–70% of those cases. The condition costs the global economy roughly $1.3 trillion annually, with about half borne by unpaid family caregivers.

> **"The WHO estimates 99% of the global population breathes air exceeding its recommended limits."**

"The WHO estimates 99% of the global population breathes air exceeding its recommended limits."

"We know more today than ever before about what drives dementia risk, and these guidelines translate that knowledge into action."

— Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General

Air Pollution Emerges as a Brain Health Threat

One of the most significant additions is the inclusion of air pollution as a modifiable risk factor. The WHO now recommends reducing exposure to fine particulate matter, specifically PM2.5 particles produced by vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, wildfire smoke and household cooking with solid fuels.

These pollutants can penetrate the body's defenses and reach the brain, triggering inflammation and oxidative stress linked to cognitive decline. The WHO estimates 99% of the global population breathes air exceeding its recommended limits. Eliminating air pollution could prevent approximately 3% of dementia cases, the report states.

The recommendation carries particular weight for India, where roughly 57% of rural households still rely on solid fuels for cooking — a primary source of household air pollution linked to cognitive impairment in older adults, according to research published in BMC Geriatrics.

From Screening to Treatment: The Hearing Aid Shift

The 2019 guidelines recommended screening for hearing loss among older adults. The 2026 update goes further, endorsing hearing aids as an intervention to reduce dementia risk.

About one in five people globally experience hearing loss, though many cases remain undiagnosed. Untreated hearing loss forces the brain to devote more resources to processing sounds, leaving fewer for memory and reasoning. It also contributes to social isolation — itself a recognised risk factor — and may cause structural brain changes.

The WHO estimates that eliminating hearing loss could prevent roughly 7% of dementia cases. A JAMA Neurology study published in August 2025 found that adults who began using hearing aids before age 70 reduced their dementia risk by up to 61%.

In India, a 2025 study from the Indian Institute of Science found hearing loss affects 41% of the population and raises the likelihood of cognitive impairment by 69%, underscoring the recommendation's public health implications for the country and its diaspora.

Supplements the WHO Says to Skip

The guidelines include a pointed warning about supplements. The WHO recommends against taking vitamins B and E, omega-3 fatty acids and multivitamin combinations for cognitive decline prevention — unless a diagnosed deficiency exists.

Despite widespread marketing claims about memory support, the agency found insufficient evidence these supplements prevent or reverse dementia. Taking them without a deficiency may carry risks including harmful nutrient buildup and negative interactions with medications, the WHO report states.

The Broader Prevention Toolkit

The guidelines also reinforce previously recommended strategies. Cognitive training receives a stronger endorsement, now recommended for adults with normal cognition and those with mild impairment. Social engagement — volunteering, maintaining relationships — is highlighted as protective. The WHO reiterates the importance of physical activity, tobacco cessation, reducing alcohol intake, healthy eating and managing hypertension, diabetes and high cholesterol.

A Lancet Commission analysis estimated 41.2% of dementia cases in India are attributable to modifiable risk factors — higher than in wealthy nations — driven by gaps in childhood education, smoking, hypertension and diabetes.

What to Watch

A Lancet Healthy Longevity study published this month found dementia risk factor patterns vary significantly across 14 countries, suggesting prevention programmes must be tailored by region. With India's population over 60 projected to reach 20% by 2050, how these guidelines are implemented at national and state levels will be closely watched.
